title: Delta
teaches: Delta estimates how much an option's price moves for a $1 move in the stock; times 100 it tells you how many shares a contract acts like, it shifts with price, time and implied volatility, and some traders read it as rough odds of finishing in the money.

facts.quote: Delta is a theoretical estimate of how much an option’s premium may change given a $1 move in the underlying.
facts.claim: Delta estimates how much an option's price may change when the stock moves $1.

facts.quote: For an option with a Delta of .50, an investor can expect about a $.50 move in that option’s premium given a $1 move, up or down, in the underlying.
facts.claim: A .50 delta option moves about 50 cents for a $1 move in the stock, up or down.

facts.quote: For purchased options owned by an investor, Delta is between 0 and 1.00 for calls and 0 and -1.00 for puts.
facts.claim: Bought calls have a delta from 0 to 1.00; bought puts from 0 to -1.00.

facts.quote: short puts have a positive Delta (technically a negative Delta multiplied by a negative number of contracts); short calls have negative Delta (technically a positive Delta times a negative number of contracts).
facts.claim: Selling flips the sign: a short put has positive delta and a short call has negative delta.

facts.quote: Long calls have positive Delta; conversely short calls have negative Delta. Long puts have negative Delta; short puts have positive Delta.
facts.claim: Long calls and short puts are positive delta; short calls and long puts are negative delta.

facts.quote: As the stock price rises and the call option goes deeper-in-the-money, Delta typically approaches 1.00 because of the increased likelihood the option will be in-the-money at expiration.
facts.claim: As a call goes deeper in the money, its delta moves toward 1.00.

facts.quote: The closer an option's Delta is to 1.00 or -1.00, the more the price of the option responds (in terms of dollars) to actual long or short stock when the underlying moves.
facts.claim: The closer delta is to 1.00 or -1.00, the more the option moves like the stock itself.

facts.quote: Stock price, days remaining to expiration and implied volatility will impact Delta.
facts.claim: Delta changes with the stock price, the days left and implied volatility.

facts.quote: With an increase in implied volatility, Delta gravitates toward .50 as more and more strikes are now considered possibilities for winding up in-the-money because of the perceived potential for movement in the underlying.
facts.claim: When implied volatility rises, deltas move toward .50.

facts.quote: Some traders view Delta as a percentage probability an option will wind up in-the-money at expiration. Therefore, an at-the-money option would have a .50 Delta or 50% chance of being in-the-money at expiration.
facts.claim: Some traders read delta as the rough odds of finishing in the money; at the money, about .50 or 50%.

facts.quote: less than a .10 Delta (or less than 10% probability of being in-the-money) is not viewed as very likely to be in-the-money at any point and will need a strong move from the underlying to have value at expiration.
facts.claim: An option under .10 delta is unlikely to finish in the money and needs a strong move to be worth anything at expiry.

facts.quote: an in-the-money call with longer time until expiration will always have a lower Delta than the same strike call with less time until expiration. It is just the opposite for out-of-the-money calls
facts.claim: Less time left means a higher delta for an in-the-money call and a lower delta for an out-of-the-money call.

facts.quote: As expiration nears, in-the-money call Deltas increase toward 1.00, at-the-money call Deltas remain around .50 and out-of-the-money call Deltas fall toward 0 provided other inputs remain constant.
facts.claim: Near expiry, in-the-money call deltas rise toward 1.00, at-the-money ones stay near .50, out-of-the-money ones fall toward 0.

facts.quote: Delta is constantly changing during market hours and will typically not accurately predict the exact change in an option’s premium.
facts.claim: Delta changes all day and usually won't predict the exact change in the option's price.

facts.quote: If share prices fall by $1, this same $20 call option would be expected to lose $.50 in value, all other pricing factors remaining constant.
facts.claim: The delta estimate assumes everything else holds still; the .50 delta call loses about 50 cents on a $1 drop.

facts.quote: Options typically do not move as much as their underlying stock unless they are deep-in-the-money and/or very close to expiration.
facts.claim: Options usually move less than the stock unless deep in the money or very near expiry.

facts.quote: A Delta of .50, for example, means that an option can be expected (all other things being equal) to move about $0.50 for every one-point move in the underlying product.
facts.claim: A .50 delta means about $0.50 for each one-point stock move, all else equal.

facts.quote: It represents roughly how much the option behaves like the underlying stock.
facts.claim: Delta shows roughly how much the option behaves like the stock.

facts.quote: Normally, if the stock price goes up and the other factors remain the same, then a call option goes higher. Therefore, if the call option has gone down, then one of the other factors must have changed.
facts.claim: If a call falls while the stock rises, something other than the stock price changed.

facts.quote: Sometimes, the market bids up the implied volatility in anticipation of a market-moving event such as earnings release or a major speech by an important person.
facts.claim: Implied volatility often gets bid up ahead of events like earnings.

facts.quote: After the event, the implied volatility often drops sharply, especially if the event failed to have the expected impact.
facts.claim: After the event, implied volatility often drops sharply.

facts.quote: The passage of time can certainly push an option's value lower. A dividend payment may also have an impact. The real wild card is implied volatility.
facts.claim: Time and dividends can push an option lower; implied volatility is the wild card.

facts.quote: a call or a put with a Delta close to 1.00 (or -1.00 for puts). This option moves very close to a 1:1 ratio with stock movement up and down, often viewed as the equivalent of long or short stock.
facts.claim: Deep in the money, delta is near 1.00 (or -1.00) and the option moves close to 1:1 with the stock.

facts.quote: The difference is that although these options move with the stock, they do not move at the same 1:1 ratio. Instead, if the stock went up $1, we could expect the 0.75 Delta calls to gain $0.75.
facts.claim: A 0.75 delta call moves with the stock but not 1:1: about $0.75 per $1.

facts.quote: Underlying stock positions will not have Gamma because their Delta is always 1.00 (long) or -1.00 (short) and will not change.
facts.claim: Stock always has a delta of 1.00 long or -1.00 short, and it never changes.

facts.quote: Positive Gamma means that the Delta of long calls will become more positive and move toward +1.00 when the stock price rises, and less positive and move toward 0 when the stock price falls.
facts.claim: A long call's delta grows toward 1.00 as the stock rises and shrinks toward 0 as it falls.

facts.quote: Greeks are not a guarantee of exact option premium changes, but rather a theoretical guidepost that gives investors an estimate of an option’s value when the underlying moves
facts.claim: The Greeks are a theoretical guide, not a guarantee of exact price changes.

facts.quote: As the price of the stock changes by $2.00, the price of the options changes by $.50 for every $1.00. Therefore the price of the options changes by (.50 x 2) = $1.00.
facts.claim: For a $2 stock move, a .50 delta option changes about .50 times 2, or $1.00.

facts.quote: The Delta is not a fixed percentage. Changes in price of stock and time to expiration affect the Delta value.
facts.claim: Delta is not fixed; the stock price and time to expiry change it.

facts.quote: Vega indicates an absolute change in option value for a 1% change in volatility.
facts.claim: Vega is the price change for a one-point (1%) change in volatility.

facts.quote: Theta indicates an absolute change in the option value for a one day reduction in time until expiration.
facts.claim: Theta is the price change from one day passing.

facts.quote: With a higher implied volatility, the same $45 call has a much lower Delta while the out-of-the-money call’s Delta increases dramatically.
facts.claim: Higher implied volatility lowers in-the-money deltas and raises out-of-the-money deltas.

facts.quote: When an investor exercises a call option, the net price paid for the underlying stock on a per share basis is the sum of the call's strike price plus the premium paid for the call.
facts.claim: A call buyer's real cost for the shares is strike plus premium, the break-even at expiry.

facts.quote: if the owner's options expire with no value, this loss can be the entire amount of the premium paid for the option.
facts.claim: If the option expires worthless, the buyer loses the whole premium.

facts.quote: A call option is in-the-money when the underlying security's price is higher than the strike price.
facts.claim: A call is in the money when the stock is above the strike.

facts.quote: As a general rule a single-stock option covers 100 shares of the underlying security
facts.claim: One stock option contract usually covers 100 shares.

facts.quote: If the option is trading at a premium of, say, $4 per share, then the aggregate premium for a single option contract would be $400.
facts.claim: Per-share option prices are multiplied by 100 for one contract: $4 a share is $400.

facts.quote: So, if the delta is .30 for a specific option contract, for each $1 move the option price may move by $0.30.
facts.claim: A .30 delta option may move about $0.30 for each $1 stock move.

facts.quote: However, an option price will not always move exactly by the amount of the delta. Delta is a dynamic greek that is constantly changing because it is impacted by other factors.
facts.claim: The option won't always move exactly by delta; delta keeps changing.

facts.quote: All else being equal, an in-the-money call option's delta will move toward 1 at expiration, and an in-the-money put option delta will move toward –1 at expiration.
facts.claim: All else equal, in-the-money deltas move toward 1 (calls) or -1 (puts) at expiry.

facts.quote: if a long call is showing a delta of .30, the trader might think of the position as if he were long 30 shares.
facts.claim: A .30 delta long call can be thought of like being long 30 shares.

facts.quote: If your long call is showing a delta of .30, some traders may think of this as having approximately a 30% probability of being in the money.
facts.claim: Some traders treat a .30 delta as roughly a 30% chance of finishing in the money.

facts.quote: Probability will be a moving target as well, because time and movement of the underlying security will adjust the percentages as you go.
facts.claim: That probability reading keeps moving as time passes and the stock moves.

facts.quote: Many traders also use delta as a gauge of the probability that an option will be ITM at expiration: A call option with a 0.30 delta suggests about a 30% chance of being ITM at expiration.
facts.claim: Many traders use delta as a rough gauge of the odds of finishing in the money: 0.30 suggests about 30%.

facts.quote: At-the-money options typically have deltas around 0.50, suggesting a 50/50 chance.
facts.claim: At-the-money options sit near 0.50 delta, about a coin flip.

facts.quote: Traders looking for the greatest traction might consider high-delta options, although these options tend to be more expensive since they're more likely to expire ITM.
facts.claim: High-delta options track the stock best but tend to cost more.

facts.quote: Some traders might use it to estimate the probability of an option expiring in the money. For example, an option with a delta of .40 can also be interpreted as having a 40% chance of expiring in the money.
facts.claim: Some traders read a .40 delta as about a 40% chance of finishing in the money.

facts.quote: One important thing to note about delta is that it doesn't have a constant rate of change. It grows as an option moves further in the money and shrinks as it moves further out of the money.
facts.claim: Delta grows as an option moves into the money and shrinks as it moves out.

facts.quote: Generally, time decay works against options buyers and favors options sellers.
facts.claim: Time decay hurts option buyers and helps sellers.

facts.quote: the Greeks and the pricing model outputs on which they are based provide theoretical values and assumes all other variables are held constant.
facts.claim: The Greeks are theoretical and assume everything else holds still.

facts.quote: This means that a call option with a delta of .40 would be expected to increase by $0.40 if the underlying rose $1.
facts.claim: A .40 delta call is expected to gain about $0.40 on a $1 rise.

facts.quote: Intrinsic value does not mean profit.
facts.claim: Being in the money is not the same as making money on the trade.

facts.quote: Options occasionally; no further rules. The premium paid is the stop.
facts.claim: Rule B25: we use options occasionally, and on an option we buy the premium paid is the stop.

facts.quote: Trade shares; options are only a defined-risk alternative.
facts.claim: Rule A6: we trade shares; options are only a defined-risk alternative.

walkthroughs.title: What delta measures
steps: Delta is your quick read on how much the option moves when the stock moves $1.
A 0.50 delta: stock up a dollar, option up about $0.50. That's with everything else held still.
Calls you buy run from 0 to 1.00. Puts you buy run from 0 to -1.00. Stock up, your put down.
Sell the option and the sign flips. A short put carries positive delta. That's the seller's side, not ours.

walkthroughs.title: Delta as shares
steps: Now make it shares. A contract is 100 shares as a general rule, so multiply by 100.
Delta times 100 is how many shares it acts like. A 0.30 delta call moves like about 30 shares.
Deep in the money, delta gets close to 1.00. Then the option moves almost like the stock itself.

walkthroughs.title: A gauge, not a promise
steps: Delta keeps changing. The stock price, the days left and implied volatility all move it.
Some traders read it as rough odds of finishing in the money. At about 0.50, that's a coin flip.
It's an estimate, not a promise. Check it again as the trade moves.

questions.q: You pull up the options chain on a name you're watching. One column says delta. What's that number telling you?
choices: Price change for a $1 stock move
Value the option loses each day
Change for a 1% move in volatility
questions.answer: Price change for a $1 stock move
questions.why: It's the price change for a $1 stock move. Say a call shows a 0.50 delta. The stock moves a dollar and the call moves about $0.50, up or down, with everything else held still. That's why I check it first. It tells me how hard the option will work for me. What it loses each day is theta, and the volatility number is vega. Different columns.
questions.lesson_line: Delta is how hard your option works when the stock moves a dollar.

wrong.Value the option loses each day: That's theta, what time costs you each day. Delta is about the stock's price.
wrong.The option's price per share: That's the premium itself. Delta tells you how the premium reacts, not what it is.
wrong.Change for a 1% move in volatility: That's vega. Delta is about the stock moving, not volatility.

questions.simple: Delta tells you roughly how much the option moves when the stock moves a dollar.

questions.q: You buy a put because you think the stock is heading lower. That put carries a positive delta.
questions.why: False. A put you buy carries a negative delta, somewhere between 0 and -1.00. You own it to make money when the stock drops, so it moves the opposite way. Stock up, your put down. Check the sign when you add it up with your shares, because the two pull against each other.
questions.lesson_line: Long calls carry positive delta. Long puts carry negative delta. Know your sign.
questions.simple: False. A put you buy makes money when the stock drops, so its delta is negative.

questions.q: You're looking at the call with its strike right at the stock price. Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: A call right at the money has a delta of about ___.
questions.why: About 0.50. Right at the money, the call moves about half as much as the stock. A $1 move up gets you roughly $0.50 a share. Some traders read that 0.50 as a coin flip to finish in the money. Go deeper in the money and delta climbs toward 1.00. Go further out and it slides toward 0. It moves with the stock, so check it again after a move.
questions.lesson_line: At the money, your call gets about half the stock's move.
questions.simple: Right at the money, delta sits near 0.50, so the call moves about half as much as the stock.

questions.q: Shares you own carry a delta of 1.00, and that never changes as the stock moves.
questions.why: True. Own the shares and every $1 move is a $1 move for you. Delta 1.00, every day, at any price. Short the shares and it's -1.00. That's the yardstick. When I compare an option with a share position, I'm asking how close it gets to that 1.00.
questions.lesson_line: Stock is the yardstick at 1.00. Every option's delta is read against it.
questions.simple: True. Shares you own move one for one with the stock, so their delta stays at 1.00.

questions.q: You bought a call and the stock kept running. Now your call is deep in the money. What's its delta doing?
questions.why: Climbing toward 1.00. The deeper in the money, the more likely the call finishes there. So it acts more and more like the shares. Near 1.00 it moves close to dollar for dollar with the stock. That's what you want on a winner. It's also why a deep call hurts almost like stock if the move reverses.
questions.lesson_line: The deeper in the money, the more your call trades like the shares.

wrong.It falls back toward 0: That's a call sliding further out of the money. Yours went the other way.
wrong.It stays put near 0.50: Around 0.50 is where a call sits at the money. Delta moves as the stock moves.
wrong.It hits 1.00 at the strike: At the strike it sits near 0.50. It climbs toward 1.00 bit by bit as the call goes deeper.

questions.simple: Deep in the money, a call's delta climbs toward 1.00, so it moves almost like the stock.

questions.q: A trader who likes the stock sells a put on it instead of buying a call. Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: Sell a put and your position's delta is ___.
questions.why: Positive. A put you buy has negative delta. Sell it and the sign flips. So the short put makes money when the stock rises and loses when it falls. It leans long, the same way as owning the shares. That's not a trade we take though. For us, options are only a defined-risk alternative to shares. A short put keeps losing the further the stock falls.
questions.lesson_line: Selling flips the sign. A short put leans long, like owning the stock.
questions.simple: Selling a put flips its sign, so your position has positive delta and gains when the stock rises.

questions.q: Your call shows a 0.40 delta, so a $1 move up in the stock will add exactly $0.40 a share.
questions.why: False. Delta is an estimate, not a quote. That 0.40 assumes everything else holds still, and it never does. Time passes, implied volatility moves, and delta itself shifts as the stock moves. So you'll land near $0.40, rarely right on it. Use it to plan the trade, then look again once the stock moves.
questions.lesson_line: Delta tells you roughly what's coming. Plan with it, then check it again.
questions.simple: False. Delta is an estimate that keeps shifting, so the real move lands near $0.40, not right on it.

deeper.trap: Trap: reading delta like a price quote. It holds every other factor still. In real markets those factors move too. Delta itself changes all day, so even a one dollar stock move usually won't give the exact estimate.

questions.q: You spot a cheap call on the chain showing a 0.20 delta. What do some traders read into that number?
choices: A 20% chance it ends in the money
A 20% gain when the stock gains 1%
A loss of $0.20 a share each day
A premium of $0.20 a share today
questions.answer: A 20% chance it ends in the money
questions.why: Roughly a 20% shot at finishing in the money. Some traders read delta as rough odds, so 0.20 is about one in five. Keep it rough. It moves every day as time passes and the stock moves. What it does tell you is this call is a long shot. If it finishes out of the money, the whole premium is gone. On an option we buy, that premium is the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Low delta, low odds. A cheap call is still a long shot.

wrong.A 20% gain when the stock gains 1%: Delta works in dollars, not percent. It's about $0.20 for each $1 the stock moves.
wrong.A loss of $0.20 a share each day: That's theta, what time costs you. Delta is about the stock's price.
wrong.A premium of $0.20 a share today: Delta isn't the price. It tells you how the price reacts to the stock.

questions.simple: Some traders read a 0.20 delta as about a 20% chance the call finishes in the money.

questions.q: Your call shows a 0.45 delta. The stock pops $2 and nothing else changes. Roughly what does the call gain, per share?
questions.why: $0.90 a share. Delta times the move: 0.45 times $2 is $0.90. Run that before you buy, so you know what a normal move is worth to you. It's a ballpark. Delta keeps shifting, so the real number lands close, not exact.
questions.lesson_line: Option move is roughly delta times stock move. Run it before you buy.
questions.simple: Delta times the move. 0.45 times $2 is about $0.90 a share.

wrong.$1.55: You took 0.45 away from $2. Delta multiplies the move.
wrong.$4.44: You divided $2 by 0.45. Delta multiplies the move.
wrong.$2.45: You added the two. Multiply them: 0.45 times $2.

questions.story: You own a put as protection, and it shows a -0.40 delta. The stock rallies $1. Nothing else changes.
questions.q: What does your put do, per share?
questions.why: It loses about $0.40 a share. Your put's delta is negative, so it moves against the stock. -0.40 times a $1 rally is about -$0.40. And since 0.40 is well short of 1.00, the put moves less than the shares do. That's the trade-off with a put. It pays when the stock drops and gives back a little when it rallies.
questions.lesson_line: Put deltas are negative. Stock up, put down, by about the delta.

wrong.Gain about $0.40 a share: You dropped the minus sign. A put pays when the stock falls, not when it rallies.
wrong.Gain about $0.60 a share: That's 1 minus 0.40, and the wrong way too. The put loses about its delta.
wrong.Lose about $0.60 a share: That's 1 minus 0.40. The put loses about its delta, 0.40, not what's left over.

questions.simple: Your put loses about $0.40 a share, because a negative delta moves against the stock.

questions.q: You're weighing one call at a 0.40 delta instead of the shares. The contract covers 100 shares. What does it trade like?
questions.why: About 40 shares. Multiply the delta by the 100 shares in the contract: 0.40 times 100 is 40. For the next $1 move, it's like holding about 40 shares. That's how I compare an option with a share position. Count what it moves like, not what it covers. It's a rough number, since delta changes as the stock moves.
questions.lesson_line: Delta times 100 tells you how many shares one contract acts like.

wrong.About 60 shares: That's 1 minus the delta. The call moves like 0.40 of the 100.
wrong.About 100 shares: That's what you'd own if you exercised. Until then it moves like about 40.

questions.simple: Delta times 100 shares is 40, so one 0.40 delta call moves like about 40 shares.

questions.story: A friend sold a call against shares he owns. The call shows a 0.35 delta. The stock rises $2. Nothing else changes.
questions.q: Looking at the call alone, what happens to it, per share?
choices: He loses about $0.70 on the call
He gains about $0.70 on the call
He loses about $0.35 on the call
He gains about $0.35 on the call
questions.answer: He loses about $0.70 on the call
questions.why: He loses about $0.70 a share on the call. Selling flips the sign, so his short call carries negative delta and a rally costs him. 0.35 times the $2 rise is about $0.70. His shares made $2 a share on the same move, so he's still ahead overall. That's the deal on a covered call. He gives up part of the upside. Covered calls aren't our thing, though. We just hold the stock.
questions.lesson_line: On a short call, every dollar up costs about the delta.

wrong.He gains about $0.70 on the call: That's the buyer's side. He sold it, so the sign flips.
wrong.He loses about $0.35 on the call: That's one dollar's worth. The stock moved $2, so double it.
wrong.He gains about $0.35 on the call: Wrong sign and only one dollar's worth. He sold the call, and the stock moved $2.

questions.simple: He sold the call, so a rally costs him. 0.35 times $2 is about $0.70 a share.

visual.title: The short call and the move

rows.label: Delta of the call he sold

questions.q: The stock rallies $1. Per share, your call should gain more dollars than the stock did.
questions.why: False. Per share, your call moves less than the stock, not more. Delta tells you how much of the move you get. A 0.75 delta call picks up about $0.75 on a $1 rally. Only deep in the money or right near expiry does it get close to the full dollar. So if your call lags the shares, nothing's broken. That's delta.
questions.lesson_line: A call that lags the stock isn't broken. That's delta at work.
questions.simple: False, because per share a call moves less than the stock. A 0.75 delta call gains about $0.75 on a $1 rally.

reasons: the statement was reversed to remove a tell

questions.story: The stock trades at 100 with 30 days to expiry. Call deltas: 95 strike 0.75, 100 strike 0.53, 105 strike 0.31, 110 strike 0.15.
questions.q: You want a call that moves about $0.30 for each $1 in the stock. Which strike do you buy?
questions.why: The 105. Its 0.31 delta gets you about $0.31 for each $1 the stock moves, right on your target. The 100 strike at 0.53 and the 110 at 0.15 both miss. The 95 is deeper in the money, so its 0.75 delta is way past what you asked for. Read the delta column first. It tells you how hard each strike works before you even look at the price.
questions.lesson_line: Read the delta column first. It tells you how hard each strike works.

wrong.The 100 strike: That's the at-the-money call at 0.53. About $0.53 per $1, well past your target.
wrong.The 110 strike: At 0.15 it moves about $0.15 per $1, about half of what you want.
wrong.The 95 strike: Lower strike, more delta. At 0.75 it moves about $0.75 per $1, more than double your target.

questions.simple: The 105 strike has a 0.31 delta, the closest to the 0.30 you want, so it moves about $0.31 per $1.

questions.q: You own 3 calls, each at a 0.55 delta. The stock rallies $4 and nothing else changes. Roughly what's the position up?
questions.why: About $660. Work it per contract first. 0.55 times $4 is $2.20 a share. One contract covers 100 shares, so that's $220. Three contracts make $660. It's a ballpark. On a $4 move delta itself shifts, so the real number drifts from the estimate. Still, run it before you buy, so you know what a normal move does to the position.
questions.lesson_line: Delta times move times 100 times contracts. The bigger the move, the rougher it gets.
questions.simple: 0.55 times $4 is $2.20 a share. Times 100 shares and 3 contracts, that's about $660.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating $660 as exact. Delta is a theoretical estimate that keeps changing, so the real gain usually differs. The bigger the move, the rougher the number.

wrong.$220: That's one contract. You own three.
wrong.$1,200: You treated the calls like shares. 3 times $4 times 100 is $1,200, but delta is 0.55, not 1.
wrong.$6,600: A decimal slipped. Redo it per contract: $220 each, three of them.

questions.q: The stock goes flat for weeks. Your in-the-money call's delta tends to rise toward 1.00 as expiry gets close.
questions.why: True. With the stock flat and everything else steady, an in-the-money call's delta climbs toward 1.00 as expiry nears. Less time left means less chance it slips back out of the money. So your call starts trading more like the shares. Out of the money it's the reverse, and delta bleeds toward 0.
questions.lesson_line: Near expiry, an in-the-money call starts acting like the shares.
questions.simple: True. Flat stock and less time left, so an in-the-money call's delta rises toward 1.00.

questions.story: You buy a call at a 0.50 delta. The next day the stock runs $5. Implied volatility hasn't budged.
questions.q: The call made more than delta times the move. Why?
choices: Time passing added to its value
Its delta shrank as the stock rose
questions.why: Its delta grew on the way up. A call's delta climbs toward 1.00 as the stock rises and the call moves into the money. So each extra dollar paid you a bit more than the last. 0.50 times $5 is only the starting rate, and it runs low on a move this big. Time works against you as a buyer, and volatility held still. Neither one helped.
questions.lesson_line: On a big move your way, your call's delta grows. The simple math runs low.

wrong.Time passing added to its value: Time works against you as a buyer. It took a little away.
wrong.Higher volatility lifted its price: Implied volatility held still, so that wasn't it.
wrong.Its delta shrank as the stock rose: Backwards. A call's delta grows toward 1.00 as the stock rises.

questions.simple: A long call's delta grows as the stock rises, so each extra dollar paid more than the one before.

deeper.trap: Trap: the 0.50 delta is only the starting rate. Over a $5 climb it keeps growing, so the average rate is higher than 0.50 and the gain beats 0.50 times $5. The same change works against you on the way down, where delta shrinks as the call moves out of the money.

questions.story: A stock trades at 100 with a month to expiry. The 115 call costs $0.22 and shows a 0.06 delta. It looks cheap.
questions.q: What does that delta tell you about the trade?
choices: It needs a strong move to pay off
Cheap, so it's the low-risk choice
It will track the stock closely
questions.answer: It needs a strong move to pay off
questions.why: It needs a strong move to pay off. Read as odds, a delta this low is under a 10% shot at finishing in the money.
questions.lesson_line: A tiny delta is a long shot. I size it like one.

wrong.Cheap, so it's the low-risk choice: Cheap per contract, but it can expire worthless and take the whole premium. Low odds aren't low risk.
wrong.It will track the stock closely: At 0.06 it barely follows the stock. A $1 move adds only about $0.06.

questions.q: You want an option that moves as close to the shares as you can get. Which delta do you look for?
choices: About 0.15, far out of the money
About 0.70, a bit in the money
questions.why: About 0.90, deep in the money. The closer delta is to 1.00, the more the option moves like the stock. At 0.90 you get nearly the full dollar on each $1 move. You pay for it though. High-delta options cost more, and they fall almost as hard as the shares. At that point, ask why you're not just buying shares. We trade shares first.
questions.lesson_line: For a stock-like option, pick a delta near 1.00 and expect to pay up.

wrong.About 0.15, far out of the money: That barely follows the stock. It's a long shot that needs a big move.
wrong.About 0.50, right at the money: That moves about half as much as the stock. Not close.
wrong.About 0.70, a bit in the money: Closer, but well short of one for one. 0.90 sits nearer 1.00, so it tracks better.

questions.simple: Pick the delta closest to 1.00. Deep in the money, the option moves almost one for one with the stock.

deeper.counter: Counter: tracking the stock has a price. High-delta options tend to be more expensive. They also move close to 1:1 on the way down. A drop hurts almost as much as owning the shares.

questions.story: The stock sits at 100 and goes nowhere for two weeks. Implied volatility holds steady. You hold the 105 call, which started near 0.31 delta.
questions.q: Where's its delta headed as expiry gets closer?
questions.why: Toward 0. The stock is sitting under your 105 strike and the clock keeps running. With everything else steady, an out-of-the-money call's delta slides toward 0 as expiry nears. Every quiet day, your call reacts less to each move in the stock. In the money it's the opposite, and delta climbs toward 1.00. Right at the money it hangs near .50. An out-of-the-money call needs the move soon.
questions.lesson_line: An out-of-the-money call needs the move soon. Every quiet day, it reacts less to the stock.

wrong.It rises toward 1.00: That's an in-the-money call. Yours sits below its strike.
wrong.It stays near 0.31: Delta isn't fixed. Time moves it even when the stock sits still.
wrong.It drifts toward 0.50: Around 0.50 is where at-the-money calls sit. Yours is out of the money, so it's not headed there.

questions.simple: Time is running out and the stock is still below the strike, so the call's delta falls toward 0.

deeper.example: Example: the 105 call began near 0.31 delta with the stock at 100. After two quiet weeks the stock has not moved, but the call has less time left to get above the strike. Its delta slides toward 0, so it reacts less and less to each stock move.

questions.q: Earnings are next week. Implied volatility jumps but the stock hasn't moved. What happens to a far out-of-the-money call's delta?
questions.why: It rises toward 0.50. Higher implied volatility means the market's pricing a bigger move. More strikes start to look like they could finish in the money. So a far out-of-the-money call's delta climbs, and a deep in-the-money call's delta comes down. After the report, implied volatility often drops sharply. Your boost can fade fast, so don't mistake it for the stock doing the work.
questions.lesson_line: Delta isn't only about price. Implied volatility moves it too.

wrong.It falls back toward 0: That's what time does as expiry nears. Higher implied volatility pushes the other way.
wrong.It stays about the same: Delta moves with implied volatility, not just with price and time left.
wrong.It leaps toward 1.00: Higher volatility pulls it toward 0.50, not 1.00. Only a deep in-the-money call sits near 1.00.

questions.simple: Higher implied volatility pulls deltas toward 0.50, so a far out-of-the-money call's delta rises.

deeper.example: Example: ahead of earnings, the market often bids up implied volatility. A far out-of-the-money call that looked like a long shot now looks possible, so its delta rises. After the report, implied volatility often drops sharply, and that pull on delta can fade.

questions.story: Before earnings you buy a call with a 0.53 delta. The stock gaps up $2 on the report. The next morning your call is worth less than you paid.
questions.q: Delta said you should be up. What most likely happened?
choices: Implied volatility fell after the news
The gap turned its delta negative
Delta only works on expiry day
A $2 gap is too small for delta
questions.answer: Implied volatility fell after the news
questions.why: Implied volatility fell after the news. Delta holds everything else still. Implied volatility often drops sharply after the event, and that can outweigh the gain from the move.
questions.lesson_line: Into earnings, delta is only part of the price. A volatility drop can beat a gap your way.

wrong.The gap turned its delta negative: A call's delta stays between 0 and 1.00. A move up makes it larger, not negative.
wrong.Delta only works on expiry day: Delta is a reading for right now, before expiry. It worked; something else changed.
wrong.A $2 gap is too small for delta: Delta works per $1 of stock move. A $2 gap is plenty for it to show.

questions.story: You buy the 105 call for $1.66. It shows a 0.31 delta. You read that as roughly a 31% chance it finishes in the money.
questions.q: Is that 31% also your rough chance of making money if you hold to expiry?
choices: Yes, same: delta says 31% to profit
questions.why: Lower. Finishing in the money only needs the stock above 105. Making money needs it above your break-even, the strike plus what you paid: 105 plus 1.66 is 106.66. Anywhere between 105 and 106.66 you're in the money and still losing. So your odds of a profit sit below the 31% some traders read off delta. The premium you paid raises the bar the stock has to clear.
questions.lesson_line: In the money isn't the same as making money. Profit needs strike plus premium.

wrong.Yes, same: it must clear 105: Above 105 is just in the money. Between 105 and 106.66 you're in the money and still losing.
wrong.No, higher: 1.66 is a cushion: The premium is your cost, not a cushion. It raises the bar the stock has to clear.
wrong.Yes, same: delta says 31% to profit: Read as odds at all, delta is about finishing in the money. Profit needs the stock past break-even.

questions.simple: No. You need the stock above 106.66 to make money, which is harder than just finishing above 105.

deeper.trap: Trap: delta, read as odds, speaks to finishing in the money, which only needs the stock above 105. Profit needs strike plus premium: 105 plus 1.66 is 106.66. A stock that ends between 105 and 106.66 finishes in the money and still loses you money. Even the in-the-money reading is rough, because it keeps moving.

questions.story: You'd normally buy 300 shares here. This time you buy 3 at-the-money calls instead, each at a 0.50 delta.
questions.q: For the next $1 move, how does that compare with your usual 300 shares?
questions.why: Like about 150 shares. Each contract covers 100 shares, but at 0.50 delta it moves like about 50 of them. Three contracts make about 150. That's half your normal exposure. Want the full size and you'd need more contracts. Me, I trade shares first. Options are an occasional tool, and the premium I pay is my stop.
questions.lesson_line: Count exposure by delta, not by contracts. Three at-the-money calls trade like about 150 shares.

wrong.Like about 300 shares: That's what you'd hold after exercising. Until then, each call moves like delta times its 100 shares.
wrong.Like about 100 shares: That's one contract's full 100. At 0.50 delta each moves like about 50, and you hold 3.
wrong.Like about 50 shares: That's one contract, 0.50 times 100. You hold 3 of them.

questions.simple: Three calls at 0.50 delta move like about 150 shares, not 300. Each one moves like half its 100 shares.

deeper.trap: Trap: counting contracts instead of delta. Three contracts cover 300 shares only if you exercise. Before that, they move like about 150. The gap cuts both ways, so on a $1 drop you lose about half of what 300 shares would lose.

conflicts: Delta as odds of finishing in the money: OIC (f10) and Schwab (f47) frame it as how 'some traders' read delta; Fidelity (f42) says 'approximately'; Investopedia (f44) says 'suggests about'. Schwab's same page also says, more firmly, that delta 'provides a theoretical measure of the options probability of expiring in-the-money'. A 2014 Fox Business column by Larry Shover ('The Urban Legend and the Options Delta') argues delta is NOT the odds of expiring in the money. Not cited (its tier is not established), but it is why every question keys only the hedged reading ('some traders', 'rough', 'approximate') and never 'delta is the probability'. A Black-Scholes check in scratch (stock 100, 30 days, IV 30%, rates 4%) gives the 105 call a 0.31 delta against a model chance of finishing in the money of about 0.28, so the reading runs a little high. q23 teaches the bigger gap: the odds of profit are lower again.

Investopedia's delta page (https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/delta.asp, James Chen) describes an in-the-money option as 'currently profitable'. That contradicts OIC and the moneyness teaching in F6.03 (being in the money is not profit); the file teaches the opposite (q23, f52). The page was read in full on 2026-11-09 (HTTP 200 to the plain client), but the quote checker's client then got 403 twice and WebFetch cannot open it, and all five facts drafted from it were redundant with OIC, Fidelity or Schwab, so the file does not cite it.

Investopedia's Greeks page (s12) says 'Delta tends to increase closer to expiration for near or at-the-money options'; OIC (f13) says at-the-money call deltas 'remain around .50' as expiry nears. The file follows OIC and cites no Investopedia fact on that point.

Investopedia's Greeks page (s12) also says higher deltas suit 'higher-risk, higher-reward strategies' and lower deltas suit 'lower-risk strategies with high win rates'. For an option buyer that reads backwards (OIC f11: under .10 delta is a long shot); it likely describes selling. Not cited.

The chains and prices in q14, q17, q18, q20, q22 and q23 are illustrative, not real quotes: they were checked for internal consistency with a Black-Scholes model in scratch (stock 100, 30 days, IV 30%, rates 4%, e.g. 95/100/105/110 calls at 0.75/0.53/0.31/0.15, and the 115 call at $0.22 with a 0.06 delta). No ticker or date is named, and no question's key depends on the model: every keyed number is a given or a calc.

Investopedia's delta-neutral page (deltaneutral.asp) has a garbled worked example (it says the hedged position 'would not be zero'), and CME Group's education pages refused the plain client (403) on 2026-11-09. Neither is cited.

Fidelity's delta article (s11) is headed 'Learn how this greek can help you assess the probability of making a profit' and ends on 'an approximation of the probability of profit', while its own body (f42) and OIC (f10) describe the odds of finishing in the money. Profit at expiry needs the stock past strike plus premium (OIC f33), so q23 keys 'lower' and names 'delta is the odds of profit' as the wrong choice; no fact cites that headline. (Checker, 2026-11-09.)
